damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Dumbledore arrives on Privet Drive and greets McGonagall
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Dumbledore as whimsical, unhurried, and gently humorous: he chuckles at the cat, mutters 'I should have known,' offers lemon drops, jokes about blushing since Madam Pomfrey complimented his earmuffs, and engages McGonagall with warm, teasing wit. The exchange is rich with personality — playful deflection, quiet authority, and genuine warmth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the entire Privet Drive conversation to a handful of functional lines. All lemon-drop comedy, the Voldemort-name lecture, the blushing/earmuffs quip, and the extended back-and-forth with McGonagall are cut. Dumbledore's opening line shifts from the book's amused 'I should have known' (said to the cat) to the film's more formal 'I should've known that you would be here, Professor McGonagall' addressed directly to her after she transforms. The playful, eccentric register is largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Privet Drive scene is the reader's first extended encounter with Dumbledore's character. The book uses it to establish his defining traits — eccentricity, warmth, dry humour, and moral gravity held in deliberate tension. The film reduces him to a functional plot-delivery figure, losing the personality foundation that makes later scenes (Mirror of Erised, hospital wing) land with full weight.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Dumbledore instructs Hagrid to leave, offers no farewell to Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Dumbledore stand with McGonagall and Hagrid for a full minute looking at the baby, after which he says 'that's that' and suggests they join the celebrations. He personally lays Harry on the doorstep, tucks the letter in the blankets, then from the corner clicks the Put-Outer back on and murmurs 'Good luck, Harry' — a private, tender moment of farewell that reveals deep feeling beneath the composed exterior.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dumbledore places Harry on the step and delivers 'Good luck, Harry Potter' as a group farewell while McGonagall and Hagrid are still present. The solitary, lingering moment Dumbledore has alone with the child at the corner — clicking the lights back on, watching from a distance — is cut entirely. Hagrid is dismissed with 'There, there, Hagrid. It's not really goodbye, after all,' which has no book equivalent and slightly diminishes the gravity.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's closing image — Dumbledore alone at the corner, watching the bundle on the step, the twinkling light gone from his eyes — is one of the few moments where his private emotional life is briefly visible. Its removal flattens his relationship with Harry's fate from something personally felt to something administratively managed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Dumbledore's justification for leaving Harry with the Dursleys
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore gives a full reasoned defence: the Dursleys are Harry's only family; he will be famous before he can walk; it would be enough to turn any boy's head; growing up away from it all until he is ready is the wisest course. He looks 'very seriously' over his half-moon glasses and persuades a sceptical McGonagall through logic and care.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dumbledore's justification is condensed to 'The only family he has' and 'He's better off growing up away from all of that. Until he is ready.' The deliberate reasoning about fame corrupting a child — the moral core of his decision — is largely cut, making the choice seem perfunctory rather than a carefully weighed judgment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Dumbledore's willingness to place a child in a cold home is one of the saga's most morally complex decisions. The book shows it as a reasoned, reluctant choice grounded in long-term thinking. The film's compression makes it appear arbitrary, reducing audience understanding of a motivation that resonates across the entire series.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 — Dumbledore's start-of-term speech (Sorting ceremony)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore rises, beams at students with arms wide open, delivers the nonsense words ('Nitwit! Blubber! Oddment! Tweak!') as his entire welcome speech, then later leads the school song with evident delight — conducting the Weasley twins' funeral-march finale and clapping loudest of all, saying 'Ah, music. A magic beyond all we do here.' Percy's bemused reaction ('I think he might have told us prefects') underlines how Dumbledore's whimsy is real, not performative.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film cuts the 'Nitwit! Blubber! Oddment! Tweak!' speech entirely. Dumbledore's first words to the assembled school are the functional start-of-term notices (the Forest, the third-floor corridor). The school song and its joyful coda are absent. Dumbledore is presented as a dignified authority figure rather than a delightfully unpredictable one.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The nonsense speech and school song are the book's primary demonstration that Dumbledore operates by his own rules, that his eccentricity is genuine and joyful, and that his relationship with the students is warm rather than merely authoritative. Cutting both removes a defining characterisation beat that makes him feel like the singular figure Hagrid and others describe him as.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 — Dumbledore at the feast; interaction with Harry after Sorting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Dumbledore give Harry a quiet, knowing acknowledgment after the Quidditch match ('Well done... nice to see you haven't been brooding about that mirror... been keeping busy... excellent...') and during the feast provides contextual warmth and gentle authority. His twinkling eyes flashing at the Weasley twins regarding the forest corridor show his awareness and indulgence of students.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film feast scene (Scene 7), Dumbledore lifts his goblet and gives Harry a slight congratulatory wave after Sorting — a visual gesture replacing any dialogue. The twinkling-eyes detail directed at the Weasley twins during the corridor warning is absent; the warning itself is delivered as a straight announcement with no accompanying wit or awareness.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but consistent flattening: the film removes small signals that Dumbledore sees everything and responds to it with amusement rather than mere authority. Each individual cut is small, but cumulatively they strip the portrait of its texture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 — Mirror of Erised conversation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore sits on the floor beside Harry, equalising their positions. He explains the mirror at length, asks Harry to think rather than just telling him, then gives the socks answer to 'what do you see?' — and the narrator notes Harry suspected Dumbledore 'might not have been quite truthful.' He asks Harry not to go looking for it again and says 'It does not do to dwell on dreams and forget to live.' He also tells Harry the mirror will be moved and mentions that Ron saw himself as head boy, demonstrating omniscience with lightness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the core explanation and the 'dwell on dreams' line but cuts Dumbledore sitting on the floor with Harry (he merely walks up and stands), cuts the socks exchange entirely, and cuts the Ron/head-boy observation. The exchange is shorter and more didactic, losing the playful depth (socks as possible deflection) and the physical gesture of equality (sitting on the floor).
damaging_scenes.explanation: The socks exchange is the clearest single illustration of Dumbledore's layered self-concealment — humour as shield, wisdom delivered obliquely. Its removal, combined with the loss of the floor-sitting gesture, makes the scene a lecture rather than a meeting between two people, reducing the warmth and complexity of his relationship with Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 — Hospital wing; Dumbledore explains the Stone and Quirrell
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore gives a long, philosophically rich conversation: he explains love's protection at length, discusses Nicolas Flamel and death with 'to the well-organised mind, death is but the next great adventure,' answers Harry's questions about Snape's motives (debt to James Potter), explains the invisibility cloak provenance with a twinkle, and deflects with 'just the one?' when Harry has more questions. He is warm, evasive about Voldemort's return question ('not today... when you are ready'), and the entire scene establishes his relationship with Harry as one of guided, partial truth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the Stone explanation, love-as-protection, and the Flamel death exchange but cuts: the Snape/James debt explanation entirely; the cloak provenance (no mention of James leaving it); the philosophical framing of death; the 'Alas, the first thing you ask me I cannot tell you' evasion about Voldemort's original motive; and the 'just the one?' exchange. The Bertie Bott's vomit-bean gag is added (no book equivalent in this scene). The conversation is noticeably shorter and less philosophically weighted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is the primary site where Dumbledore's relationship with Harry is established as one of careful, loving partial disclosure — telling Harry some truths, withholding others with stated reasons, and doing so with warmth and humour. Cutting the Snape explanation also removes a key piece of Snape's arc. The loss of the cloak provenance severs a James Potter connection. Together these cuts meaningfully reduce Dumbledore's relational and narrative function in the adaptation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 — End-of-year feast; House Cup ceremony
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore's speech includes 'Yes, yes, well done, Slytherin' before pivoting to last-minute points, the 'there are all kinds of courage' framing for Neville's award, and a clapping of hands that transforms the decorations. He radiates theatrical delight in upending the expected outcome. His earlier Christmas dinner appearance (flowered bonnet, chuckling at Flitwick's joke) also adds festive eccentricity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the structure of the House Cup scene faithfully, including 'it takes a great deal of bravery to stand up to your enemies, but a great deal more to stand up to your friends' and the banner transformation. This scene is largely faithful. The Christmas dinner detail (flowered bonnet) is absent but that is a minor omission.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor: the Christmas bonnet detail is a small eccentric touch absent from the film. The House Cup scene itself is well-executed and causes minimal damage.

main_damage_causes: Systematic removal of Dumbledore's whimsical, eccentric personality markers (nonsense speech, school song, lemon drops, socks exchange, earmuffs quip) that collectively define his distinctive voice and distinguish him from a generic wise mentor

Compression of key dialogue scenes (Privet Drive, hospital wing) that establish the texture of Dumbledore's relationship with Harry — partial truths delivered with warmth, philosophical depth, and deliberate evasiveness — reducing him to a functional plot-explainer

Loss of small but cumulative physical and tonal details (sitting on the floor with Harry, solitary farewell at the corner, twinkling eyes at the twins) that signal Dumbledore's emotional investment and omniscient-yet-indulgent awareness, flattening a layered portrait into dignified authority
